analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing employees and consumers to give up their day in court before a dispute happens.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most companies make workers and customers sign contracts agreeing in advance that any future dispute—over wages, discrimination, faulty products, or fees—will be decided by a private arbitrator chosen under company-friendly rules, with no judge and no appeal. The bill would make those mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes. People could still agree to arbitrate, but only after a dispute actually arises, when they know what they're giving up. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers who currently sign away their right to sue. Under the bill, they could take workplace discrimination, wage theft, consumer fraud, and civil rights claims to a public court with a judge, juries, precedents, and appeals—instead of private arbitration where proceedings are confidential, decisions are rarely appealable, and class actions are typically barred.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers forced into arbitration

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration agreement would be valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights dispute [S2] [S3].

The bill preserves arbitration when someone voluntarily agrees to it after a dispute has arisen, and leaves labor union collective bargaining arbitration intact—while ensuring union arbitration cannot waive an employee's right to enforce constitutional or statutory rights in court [S3].
It puts court, not an arbitrator, in charge of deciding whether the law applies to an agreement, closing a common workaround where arbitrators decide their own power [S3].
The bill's findings state that most consumers and employees have little or no meaningful choice whether to arbitrate and are often unaware they have given up their rights [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on forced arbitration—large employers, banks and lenders, cable, telecom and other consumer businesses—and the arbitration industry that administers those cases. They would face the cost of defending claims in open court, including class actions and jury verdicts that public exposure to court makes more likely.

drawbacks.text: Companies would lose a predictable, cheaper dispute process; arbitration is often faster and less expensive than litigation, and employers argue courts and juries raise the cost of doing business and the price of goods and services [S3].

Some arbitrations favor workers and consumers, and voluntary post-dispute arbitration—an option the bill preserves—can still be a reasonable forum, so critics see a blanket ban as removing a useful alternative, not just an abusive one [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a one-sided practice: companies write arbitration clauses into contracts workers and consumers must accept to get a job or a product, and the bill's own findings concede there is little meaningful choice in the matter [S3]. The cost falls on businesses, which lose a cheaper, private forum and face greater class action and jury exposure. The main design tradeoff is that it bans even arbitration terms that might be fair, rather than regulating them—but it leaves genuinely voluntary, post-dispute arbitration untouched [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 22, 2018 with 32 cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S4] [S5].
The full action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action of any kind after the referral [S5].
Congress ended January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that require workers and consumers to sign away their court rights, and the arbitration industry that administers those cases, are better off because the bill never advanced; workers and consumers keep the clauses they would have lost.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent—31 Democrats and 1 Independent—and no Republican sponsored it, so support was entirely on one side of the aisle [S4].

industries.note: The multi-billion-dollar arbitration industry exists largely because of mandatory clauses in employment and consumer contracts. Banning predispute agreements for the covered disputes would eliminate most of its consumer and employment caseload.

industries.industry: Large employers and consumer-facing corporations (banks, lenders, telecom, retail)
industries.note: These companies use forced arbitration to resolve wage, discrimination, and consumer disputes privately, cheaply, and confidentially, and to block class actions. The bill would expose them to open-court litigation, juries, and class certification.
Public court litigation, including class actions, becomes available again for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights claims, expanding work for lawyers who represent individuals.
